fields.h1: Build a KYC Workflow With a Case File for Every Customer
fields.hero_description: Build a KYC workflow that opens a case for each new customer, sends every check to a named reviewer, and logs each decision.
fields.features_heading: Six Parts of a KYC Workflow Emergent Builds
fields.features_subheading: Each new customer gets one case that fills in as checks come back and reviewers decide.
fields.feature_1:
One form, one case per new customer

Emergent builds the intake form and the case database from your prompt. Each new customer's answers and uploads become one case, saved in a database you own and can query.
fields.feature_2:
ID documents read into fields

The app reads the name, birth date, and ID number from an uploaded license or passport. A field it is unsure of goes to a person, and each one is compared with what was typed.
fields.feature_3:
Your screening service, connected

Emergent connects the app to the verification or screening service you already use, through its API. Each result lands on the case, and a possible match keeps the account on hold.
fields.feature_4:
Risk ratings from rules you write

Write the factors your compliance team rates on, such as account type or expected monthly volume, and the app scores each case. A high rating goes to a senior reviewer.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts that carry a case number only

Reviewers get a Slack or email alert that names the case and links to it. Documents and birth dates stay in the database, and a case left overdue escalates to a manager you name.
fields.feature_6:
The KYC app's code, in your GitHub

Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Anyone on your team can trace each screening and routing rule to the exact lines of code that run it in production.

fields.usecase_heading: Where a KYC Case Stops for a Person
fields.tab_content_1:
With a mismatched birth year, case K-1182 waits for Leontyne

Quenmore Credit Union asks each new member for a name, birth date, address, and ID number, plus a driver's license photo. On case K-1182 the app reads 1984 from the license, but the form says 1987. The case waits for analyst Leontyne Bartholdy, whose Slack alert carries only the case number and a link.
fields.tab_content_2:
Owners with at least 25 percent each get an ID link

Ridgemoor Community Bank opens a business account for Dunmarrow Coffee Roasters, which lists three owners. The bank wants an ID from anyone owning at least 25 percent, so Gwendolen Strathearn and Prudencia Nwosu-Hart each get an ID link by email. Ottokar Granholm owns less and is recorded without one.
fields.tab_content_3:
Benedikta Talmadge clears one possible match by birth year

A Saltreach Wealth Partners client opens a brokerage account, and the connected screening service returns 1 possible match on case K-2207. The account stays on hold. Reviewer Benedikta Talmadge sees the listed person was born in 1958 and the client in 1992. She clears the match and saves her note to the case.
fields.tab_content_4:
Nine customers who never answered go to Cordelio

Corvellan Payments reviews high-risk customers every 12 months, medium every 24, and low every 36. In March, 46 come due, and each customer gets an email link to confirm their address and occupation. Within 14 days, 37 confirm. The other 9 go to the queue of analyst Cordelio Achebe-Lowe.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a KYC Workflow
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan the checks in a KYC workflow and who reviews each case, then build and test it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List what each kind of customer sends
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick the ID documents the app reads
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Put the risk factors in plain sentences
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down the fields and uploads for individuals and for companies. Mark which must be in before an account opens and which can follow. Your compliance team owns this list, and every item becomes a field or an upload on the intake form.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Choose the ID documents you accept, such as a driver's license or a passport, and the fields to read from each. Decide who checks a field the app reads with low confidence before the case moves on.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Name the identity verification and screening services you already use. Emergent connects the app to each one through its API, so every result lands on the case. Decide which results hold an account and which only add a note.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Describe each risk factor, such as expected monthly volume or the customer's country, and the rating each combination earns. Plain sentences in the prompt mean anyone on the team can read the rules the app applies to every case.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Name an owner for each kind of case
fields.howto_step_5_des: Give mismatches to an analyst and high ratings or possible matches to a senior reviewer. Pick how many days a case can sit before it moves to a manager, and require a note on every clear or escalate decision.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Set the review schedule by rating
fields.howto_step_6_des: Choose how often each rating gets a periodic review and what customers confirm in it. Then pick how many days to wait for an answer before the case lands in an analyst's queue.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before real customers see it, run 20 sample cases: clean ones, mismatches, a business with several owners, and a possible match. Have your compliance team check each decision and case record, and change the rules by prompting until they agree.

faq_plan.a: A KYC workflow is the sequence a business runs to confirm who a new customer is before opening an account. KYC stands for know your customer. The workflow collects documents and checks them, then screens the name and records every decision. It keeps going after onboarding with periodic reviews.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a KYC workflow?
faq_plan.a: Start from your compliance team's checklist: what every customer type provides, which checks run, and who decides each exception. Describe that checklist in a prompt to Emergent's AI automation builder. Emergent builds the app from that prompt, with a queue for each reviewer, and you change any rule later by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: Which parts of KYC automation still need a person?
faq_plan.a: Every exception still needs a person. KYC automation can collect details, read ID documents into fields, call your screening service, and score risk, but a person should decide a name mismatch, a possible watchlist match, or a high rating. In the app Emergent builds, each of those decisions records who made it and why.

faq_plan.q: Does an account stay on hold during a KYC workflow?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you set it to. You choose which open checks block the account, such as a missing owner ID or a possible match, and which only add a task for later. A hold that lifts only on a named sign-off works like a quality hold in manufacturing workflow automation, where a batch waits for one person.

faq_plan.q: What customer information does a KYC workflow collect?
faq_plan.a: For a US bank, the CIP rule in 31 CFR 1020.220 says the bank must obtain, at a minimum, a customer's name, date of birth, address, and identification number prior to opening an account. Other businesses write their own list with counsel. Add any fields your risk rules use, such as occupation or expected monthly volume.

faq_plan.q: How long does a KYC workflow keep records after an account closes?
faq_plan.a: For a US bank's CIP identifying information, the answer is five years after closing: 31 CFR 1020.220 says to keep it for five years after the date the account is closed. Confirm the period for your business with your compliance team, and the app keeps each case's documents and decisions until then.

faq_plan.q: How does a KYC workflow handle business customers and their owners?
faq_plan.a: It collects the owners as well as the business. Under 31 CFR 1010.230, a beneficial owner is each individual who owns at least 25 percent of the equity interests of a legal entity customer. It is also a single individual with significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct that customer. For client intake without identity checks, see agency workflow automation.

faq_plan.q: What does a KYC workflow do when screening returns a possible match?
faq_plan.a: It holds the case for a reviewer. The reviewer compares the customer's details, such as birth date and country, with the listed person's, then clears or escalates the match with a note. Banks have a specific duty here: under 31 CFR 1020.220, the CIP must include procedures for determining whether the customer appears on any list of known or suspected terrorists.

faq_plan.q: Should KYC workflow alerts include the customer's documents?
faq_plan.a: No. Keep IDs and birth dates inside the case. Send only the case number, the kind of check that failed, and a link, and the details stay behind your app's login. Emergent builds the Slack or email alert to carry exactly the fields you name in the prompt and nothing else.

faq_plan.q: How often should a KYC workflow refresh customer information?
faq_plan.a: As often as each customer's risk rating calls for. The bank due diligence rule, 31 CFR 1020.210, calls for ongoing monitoring to maintain and update customer information on a risk basis. Pick an interval for each rating with your compliance team. Expiring IDs run on the same kind of clock as insurance certificates in construction workflow automation.

plan.angle: The top results are vendor guides that list KYC stages (identification, due diligence, screening, monitoring) and sell verification software. This page shows the case-handling app around those checks: an intake form that opens a case, an ID document read into fields and compared with what the customer typed, beneficial owners collected for business accounts, possible watchlist matches held for a named reviewer, and periodic reviews scheduled by risk rating, with alerts that carry a case number and a link instead of documents. Regulatory facts are quoted from 31 CFR; the page never promises compliance, and the bank's compliance team sets every rule.
